individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces LSEP, a training regularization for diffusion transformers that integrates a linear probe into intermediate layers to promote linear separability of representations during training. This avoids the need for large pretrained external encoders or explicit representation alignment. It proposes several techniques: class-conditioning for the probe, random cropping, and time-dependent weighting. Experiments on ImageNet with SiT models show improved training efficiency and generation quality, achieving FID 1.46 with CFG, comparable to alignment-based methods. The method also combines well with REPA.
Strengths: Novel integration of linear probing as a training objective, not just evaluation.
No external encoder required, making it computationally more accessible than REPA.
Thorough ablation studies of key design choices.
Demonstrated improvements across model sizes (B, L, XL) and synergy with alignment-based methods.
Clear writing and organization.
Weaknesses: Requires class labels for the linear probe, limiting applicability to class-conditional tasks or tasks where labels are available.
Hyperparameters (crop size, weight schedule, learning rate) are tuned per model size, suggesting potential overfitting.
No theoretical analysis explaining why linear separability helps generation.
The best reported FID (1.46) relies on careful selection of CFG settings (guidance interval), which may be cherry-picked.
The comparison with REPA is not entirely apples-to-apples: REPA uses external encoders, while LSEP uses labels; the paper could discuss the trade-offs more explicitly.
Questions: How does LSEP affect training time and memory overhead compared to baseline?
Is the linear probe needed at inference time, or is it only for training?
Would LSEP work in unconditional or text-to-image settings without labels? Could it use self-supervised pseudo-labels?
What is the sensitivity to the choice of target depth across different architectures?
Does linear separability correlate with FID improvement in a causal way, or is it just a side effect?
Limitations: Reliance on class labels as supervision for the linear probe.
Experiments only on ImageNet class-conditional generation; no other datasets or modalities.
Hyperparameter selection seems architecture-specific.
Lack of theoretical justification for why linear separability improves generation.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes LSEP, a training regularization method that promotes linear separability of intermediate diffusion transformer representations by inserting a trainable linear probe into an intermediate layer. Unlike representation alignment methods (e.g., REPA), LSEP does not require external pretrained encoders or explicit alignment, and it integrates linear probing directly into the training objective. The method includes several design choices: unconditional class conditioning for the probe, random cropping of feature maps, and time-dependent weighting of the classification loss. Experiments on SiT-B/L/XL for class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 show improved training efficiency and generation quality, achieving an FID of 1.46 with CFG, surpassing prior no-external-encoder methods and approaching alignment-based approaches. LSEP also combines synergistically with REPA.
Strengths: Simple and parameter-efficient alternative to representation alignment, avoiding the need for large pretrained external encoders.
Consistent FID improvements across SiT-B/L/XL at 400K iterations and state-of-the-art FID of 1.46 without external encoders when using CFG.
Thorough ablations of key design choices: conditioning probability, target depth, random cropping, and time-dependent weighting.
Demonstrates complementarity with REPA, indicating that linear separability and alignment improve representations through distinct mechanisms.
Provides linear probing, t-SNE, and PCA analyses supporting the claim of improved linear separability.
Weaknesses: Table 2 (FID comparisons without CFG) is referenced but not included, making some quantitative claims difficult to verify.
The exact implementation of time-dependent weighting in the total loss is unclear: Eq. (6) uses a constant ω_class, but the schedule is introduced later without specifying how they are combined.
Architectural details of the linear probe branch (normalization, pooling, crop sizes) are described but not fully specified for reproduction.
The paper lacks a theoretical explanation for why linear separability improves generation; the relationship is empirical.
Hyperparameters such as the linear probe learning rate differ across model sizes (0.03 for SiT-B vs 0.0001 for others) without clear justification.
Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; generalization to other modalities or resolutions is not demonstrated.
Questions: How is the time-dependent weighting schedule applied to the loss in Eq. (6)? Is ω_class replaced by ω_class(t,k) during training?
What is the extra computational cost and memory overhead of training with LSEP compared to baseline?
Are the linear probe parameters discarded at inference, leaving the final model identical to baseline in parameter count?
How exactly does random cropping interact with the linear classifier? Is the classifier trained on cropped or full feature maps, and is the crop size sampled per iteration?
Why does the SiT-B model require a much higher learning rate for the linear probe (0.03) than the larger models (0.0001)?
Could LSEP be extended to unconditional generation or text-to-image settings where class labels are not available?
Limitations: Only evaluated on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; applicability to text-to-image, video, and higher-resolution generation is unknown.
Requires class labels during training, which may be unavailable in many datasets.
The headline FID improvement relies on CFG with a tuned guidance interval; gains without CFG are modest and not fully tabulated.
No analysis of failure cases or sensitivity to hyperparameters beyond the provided ablations.
Does not investigate CNN-based diffusion architectures, though the method is in principle architecture-agnostic.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes LSEP, a training regularization method for diffusion transformer models that promotes linear separability of intermediate representations by inserting a trainable linear probe into an intermediate layer and jointly optimizing it with the denoising objective. This eliminates the need for external pretrained encoders or explicit representation alignment. The method introduces several techniques: using unconditional class conditioning for the probe, random cropping of intermediate feature maps, and time-dependent weighting of the classification loss. Experiments on ImageNet 256 with SiT models show improved training efficiency and generation quality, achieving an FID of 1.46 with classifier-free guidance, surpassing other methods that do not rely on external encoders and closely matching alignment-based approaches like REPA. The paper also shows that LSEP can be combined with REPA for additional improvements.
Strengths: Simple and effective idea that repurposes linear probing as a training objective, removing the need for large pretrained encoders and explicit alignment.
Thorough ablations of the proposed components (conditioning probability, target depth, random cropping, time-dependent weighting) with clear analysis.
Consistent FID improvements over baseline SiT across model sizes and iteration counts, with competitive-or-better performance versus REPA at matched training budgets.
Reaches state-of-the-art FID (1.46 with CFG) among methods that do not use external visual encoders, and shows complementary gains when combined with REPA.
Provides visual and quantitative evidence (linear probing, t-SNE, PCA) that LSEP improves linear separability of intermediate features.
Weaknesses: The method is demonstrated only for class-conditional ImageNet generation; its applicability to unconditional generation, text-to-image, or label-free settings is not explored.
Key design choices, such as target depth, random crop range, and time-dependent weight schedules, are empirically tuned per model size and may not transfer easily to other architectures or datasets.

The paper does not compare against other auxiliary objectives (e.g., contrastive losses, MLP heads) to isolate whether the benefit is specifically from linear separability or simply from an auxiliary classification task.
No theoretical analysis is provided for why promoting linear separability accelerates denoising or improves generation quality, leaving the underlying mechanism somewhat unclear.
The random cropping and time-dependent weighting heuristics add complexity, and the sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not fully characterized.
Questions: How does LSEP perform on unconditional generation or on text-to-image diffusion models where class labels are unavailable?
What is the sensitivity of the optimal target depth and random crop range to different architectures (e.g., CNN-based diffusion models) and datasets?
Could the observed gains be equally attributed to the added capacity of the linear probe or to the auxiliary classification signal rather than to linear separability per se?
Does the linear probe need to be trained jointly with the diffusion model, or could it be trained in a separate stage with the same effect?
Is the time-dependent weighting of the classification loss essential, or would a constant weight with a scheduled decay work as well?
What happens to the linear probe after training? It is discarded, so how does the final model retain the benefits without the probe at inference?
Limitations: Only class-conditional generation is addressed; the method requires labels, limiting use in label-scarce or unconditional settings.
The method is evaluated only on 256x256 ImageNet; scalability to higher resolutions or more diverse datasets is not tested.
The linear probe is only used during training and does not add inference cost, but the extra training overhead and hyperparameter tuning may offset some efficiency gains.
The paper does not provide theoretical justification for the effectiveness of linear separability, nor does it analyze failure cases.
Potential negative societal impacts of improved image generation are not discussed, though these are shared with other generative models.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper proposes LSEP, a training regularization for diffusion transformers that inserts a trainable linear probe into an intermediate layer and jointly optimizes a classification loss with the denoising objective, thereby promoting linear separability of early-stage representations. It introduces three techniques: unconditional/random class conditioning for the probe branch, random cropping of intermediate feature maps, and a time-dependent piecewise-constant weight on the classification loss. Experiments on SiT models for ImageNet 256x256 show faster convergence, improved FID (1.46 with CFG and guidance interval for SiT-XL without an external encoder), and synergistic gains when combined with REPA.
Strengths: The idea of repurposing linear probing from a post-hoc evaluation tool into an explicit training regularizer is novel and clearly motivated by prior correlations between linear separability and generation quality.

Strong empirical results: LSEP achieves FID 1.46 on ImageNet 256 without relying on a pretrained external encoder, outperforming prior no-external-encoder methods and approaching alignment-based methods like REPA.
The paper provides careful ablations of its three proposed components (conditioning, random cropping, time-dependent weighting), giving useful insights into their individual contributions.
Demonstrates that LSEP can be combined with REPA to further improve performance, indicating complementary mechanisms.
Training efficiency gains are shown: LSEP reaches lower FID in fewer iterations than the baseline SiT, which is practically valuable.
Weaknesses: The implementation of 'classification-specific conditioning for the linear probe branch' is not clearly described. It is ambiguous whether this requires a separate forward pass, a separate class embedding injected into the probe, or some other mechanism; the referenced figures are redacted, making the architecture hard to reproduce.
The method is only evaluated on SiT flow-matching transformers. It is unclear whether the benefits transfer to other diffusion backbones such as DiT, U-Net, or latent diffusion models.
The paper lacks a theoretical explanation for why promoting linear separability should improve the denoising objective; the contribution is purely empirical.

The comparison with alignment-based methods is not exactly apples-to-apples: LSEP uses ground-truth class labels (available in class-conditional generation), while external encoders like DINOv2 are self-supervised. This difference in supervision is not discussed or controlled.

No baseline is provided with a nonlinear probe or an alternative auxiliary loss (e.g., contrastive) under the same conditioning scheme, so it is not clear that linearity of the probe is the key factor rather than simply adding extra supervision.
The presented Table 1 is garbled due to LaTeX color formatting, making it difficult to read the exact ablation numbers, and the paper does not report variance or multiple seeds for the main results.
Questions: How is the class conditioning for the linear probe branch implemented precisely? Does the model require a separate forward pass with a different class label, or is a separate class embedding added to the pooled features before the linear layer?

In the classification loss, is the ground-truth class label always used as the target even when the network is conditioned on the unconditional or a random class? If so, how does the classifier avoid exploiting the conditioning as a shortcut?

Did the authors compare LSEP with a nonlinear probe (e.g., an MLP head) under the same conditioning, random-crop, and time-weighting tricks to confirm that linear separability specifically is the driver of the gains?
What is the exact computational overhead of LSEP in terms of extra forward passes, memory, and training time compared to baseline SiT and REPA?
Why is the learning rate for the linear probe set to 0.03 for SiT-B but 1e-4 for SiT-L and SiT-XL? How sensitive are the results to this hyperparameter?

Do the benefits of LSEP hold for unconditional generation (i.e., when class labels are not used at sampling time)? The no-CFG results in Table 2 appear to be class-conditional but without guidance; is that correct?

Could the improvement be due to the classification loss acting as a general regularizer (e.g., reducing overfitting) rather than specifically improving linear separability? What happens if the classifier is trained with random labels?
Limitations: The method relies on class labels, which may not be available in fully unsupervised or text-to-image settings.
Evaluation is limited to 256x256 ImageNet class-conditional generation; the paper does not test text-to-image, video, higher resolution, or other datasets.
The paper does not provide a theoretical justification for why linear separability improves generation quality, leaving the mechanism as an empirical observation.
Only SiT-based flow-matching transformers are considered; applicability to CNN-based diffusion models or other transformer variants is not demonstrated.
The paper does not report statistical significance or multiple seeds, so the robustness of the FID improvements is not established.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_5

review.Summary: The paper introduces LSEP, a training regularization for flow-based diffusion transformers that promotes linear separability of intermediate representations by jointly training a linear probe with the denoising objective. The method avoids external encoders or representation alignment, and includes several technical contributions: class-conditioning design for the probe, random cropping of intermediate features, and time-dependent weighting of the classification loss. Experiments on ImageNet 256x256 with SiT models show improved training efficiency and generation quality, achieving an FID of 1.46 with classifier-free guidance without external encoders, and further gains when combined with REPA.
Strengths: Proposes a novel training strategy that repurposes linear probing as a regularizer, avoiding dependency on large pretrained encoders.
Comprehensive ablations and analysis of each proposed component (conditioning, random cropping, time weighting).
Demonstrates consistent improvements across SiT-B/L/XL and strong final FID among methods without external encoders.
Shows synergy with REPA, indicating complementary mechanisms and providing further evidence for the importance of representation geometry.
Weaknesses: Lacks comparison to a simple auxiliary classifier baseline, making it unclear whether the gains come from the proposed techniques or just from adding a classification loss.
The architecture and conditioning of the linear probe branch are inadequately described; it is unclear how class embeddings are incorporated into the probe.
The paper contains formatting issues (redacted figures, malformed tables) and inconsistent reporting of training iterations vs epochs, hurting reproducibility.
Method requires class labels, which limits its applicability to unconditional or text-to-image generation.
The final FID of 1.46 is still worse than REPA (1.42) with an external encoder, so the headline 'state-of-the-art' should be qualified to the no-external-encoder setting.
Questions: Can you provide a detailed diagram or pseudocode of the linear probe branch, specifically how the class embedding is injected? Does the probe share the diffusion model's class embedding or use a separate one?
What would be the effect of replacing the proposed probe with a standard auxiliary classifier that uses the same conditioning as the denoiser? Would it achieve similar FID?
What is the FID of the final model without classifier-free guidance at the same training length, to isolate the effect of guidance scheduling?
What is the additional computational overhead of LSEP in terms of wall-clock time and memory compared to baseline SiT training?
How sensitive are the hyperparameters (unconditional probability, crop range, time-weighting) across different model sizes and datasets? Were they tuned separately for each model?
Limitations: The method is only evaluated on class-conditional ImageNet generation; its applicability to text-to-image or unconditional tasks is unknown.
The mechanism linking linear separability to generation quality is not rigorously analyzed; further theoretical or empirical study is needed.
The paper does not report training wall-clock times or FLOPs, making it difficult to assess the claimed efficiency gains.

review.Summary: The paper introduces LSEP, a training regularization for diffusion transformers that inserts a trainable linear probe into an intermediate layer and jointly optimizes a classification loss with the denoising objective, promoting linear separability of intermediate representations without the need for large pretrained external encoders. The method includes several design choices: unconditional class conditioning for the probe, random cropping of intermediate features, and time-dependent weighting. Experiments on ImageNet 256x256 with SiT models show improved training efficiency and generation quality, achieving FID 1.46 with classifier-free guidance, comparable to alignment-based methods like REPA, and further gains when combined with REPA.
Strengths: Novel repurposing of linear probing as a training objective, avoiding dependency on external pretrained encoders.
Consistent FID improvements across SiT-B/L/XL and state-of-the-art FID (1.46 with CFG) among methods without external encoders.
Thorough ablations of key design choices (conditioning probability, target depth, random cropping, time-dependent weighting).
Demonstrates synergy with REPA, suggesting complementary mechanisms and further evidence for representation geometry.
Parameter-efficient approach with no inference overhead, as probes are discarded after training.
Provides quantitative and visual evidence of improved linear separability via linear probing, t-SNE, and PCA.
Weaknesses: Requires class labels, limiting applicability to class-conditional tasks or datasets where labels are unavailable.
Hyperparameters (crop size, weight schedule, learning rate) are tuned per model size, raising concerns about overfitting and generalizability.
Lacks theoretical analysis explaining why linear separability improves generation quality.
Comparison with REPA is not apples-to-apples: LSEP uses ground-truth labels while REPA uses self-supervised external encoders, and this trade-off is not discussed.
Implementation details of the linear probe conditioning and time-dependent weighting are unclear; formatting issues in tables and figures impede reproducibility.
No baseline with a nonlinear probe or alternative auxiliary loss to isolate whether the benefit is specifically from linear separability or just an auxiliary classification signal.
Evaluation limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; no experiments on unconditional, text-to-image, video, or higher-resolution generation.
Questions: How is the class conditioning for the linear probe branch implemented exactly? Does it require a separate forward pass with a different class label, or is a separate class embedding injected into the probe?
What is the extra computational cost and memory overhead of LSEP during training compared to baseline SiT and REPA?
How is the time-dependent weighting schedule applied to the classification loss? Is the constant ω_class in Eq. (6) replaced by a time-dependent function during training?
Is the linear probe discarded at inference, leaving the final model identical in architecture to the baseline?
Why is the learning rate for the linear probe 0.03 for SiT-B but 1e-4 for SiT-L and SiT-XL? How sensitive are results to this hyperparameter?
Would LSEP extend to unconditional or text-to-image settings where class labels are not available? Could self-supervised pseudo-labels be used?
What would be the effect of replacing the proposed linear probe with a standard auxiliary classifier or nonlinear MLP head under the same conditioning and weighting schemes?
Limitations: Method relies on class labels, restricting applicability to label-free settings.
Only evaluated on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; generalization to other datasets, modalities, or resolutions is unknown.
No theoretical justification linking linear separability to improved denoising or generation.
Hyperparameters appear architecture-specific and were tuned separately for each model size.
Does not compare against other auxiliary losses (e.g., contrastive, MLP) to establish that linear separability is the key factor.
No statistical significance or multiple seeds reported for main FID results.
Headline FID improvement relies on tuned CFG guidance interval, and gains without CFG are modest.
